questions.q: Why is Partial<User> a poor type for the body of a "customer edits their profile" request?
questions.explain: Partial keeps every key and makes it optional. A profile patch should allow only the editable fields: Partial<Pick<User, "name" | "phone">>, backed by runtime code that copies only those fields.
options: Because it allows every field of User, including role and id, so the type itself permits privilege escalation
Because Partial cannot be used on interfaces

questions.q: For interface Options { pageSize?: number }, what is Required<Options>["pageSize"]?
questions.explain: Required is { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }. The -? modifier removes the optional mark and the undefined that it added.

questions.q: const user: Readonly<User>, where User has name: string and address: { city: string }. Which line compiles?
questions.explain: Readonly is shallow: it marks the properties of User, so address cannot be replaced, but the object inside it keeps its own, writable city.

questions.q: What does Readonly<T> do at runtime?
questions.explain: All types are erased. For a runtime guarantee, use Object.freeze (which is also shallow).
options: Nothing: it is erased, and only stops assignments at compile time

questions.q: What happens with type PublicUser = Omit<User, "passwrodHash"> (a typo)?
questions.explain: Omit's key parameter is constrained to keyof any, not keyof T, so any string is accepted. Pick checks its keys. A StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> fixes it.
options: A compile error: the key does not exist
It compiles, omits nothing, and PublicUser still has passwordHash
It omits every key that starts with "pass"

questions.q: Which definition matches the standard library's Omit?
questions.explain: "Omit these keys" is "pick every key that is not one of them". Exclude removes the omitted keys from the key union, and Pick builds the object.
options: type Omit<T, K extends keyof any> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>
type Omit<T, K> = T extends K ? never : T
type Omit<T, K extends keyof T> = Exclude<T, K>

questions.q: type Payment = { id: string; kind: "card"; last4: string } | { id: string; kind: "wallet"; phone: string }. What is Omit<Payment, "id">?
questions.explain: keyof of a union gives only the shared keys (id and kind), so the result is one flattened object with just kind. The union and its member-specific fields are lost. A distributive version applies Omit to each member.
options: { kind: "card"; last4: string } | { kind: "wallet"; phone: string }

questions.q: Why does type DistributiveOmit<T, K extends keyof any> = T extends unknown ? Omit<T, K> : never keep the union intact?
questions.explain: T extends unknown is always true; its only job is to trigger distribution. The results for each member are joined back into a union.
options: Because a conditional type on a bare type parameter is applied to each union member separately, so each member is omitted on its own
Because never merges the members back together

questions.q: const labels: Record<"customer" | "staff" | "admin", string> = { customer: "Customer", staff: "Staff" }; What does the compiler say?
questions.explain: Record<K, V> is { [P in K]: V }: one required property per key. That is why it is great for lookup tables over a union: adding a role forces a new label.
options: That property admin is missing: a Record over a union of keys needs every key
That Record cannot use string literal keys

questions.q: With const stock: Record<string, number> = { rice: 12 };, what is the type of stock.garri (without noUncheckedIndexedAccess)?
questions.explain: Record<string, number> promises a number for every string key. The promise is false for missing keys. noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds | undefined to such reads; a Map is another option.
options: number, even though it is undefined at runtime
A compile error: garri does not exist

questions.q: What is Exclude<"pending" | "paid" | "cancelled", "cancelled" | "refunded">?
questions.explain: Each member of the first union is tested: kept unless it is assignable to the second. "refunded" is simply never matched; Exclude does not check that the excluded members exist.
options: A compile error, because "refunded" is not in the first union

questions.q: What does Extract<Payment, { kind: "card" }> give, for a discriminated union Payment?
questions.explain: Extract keeps the members assignable to the second type. The card member has kind: "card" plus other fields, so it is assignable to { kind: "card" } and is kept whole.
options: The member of Payment whose kind is "card", with all its fields

questions.q: The standard library defines NonNullable<T> as T & {}. Why does that work?
questions.explain: {} accepts strings, numbers, objects and every other non-nullish value. Intersecting with it keeps those and drops null and undefined, even for a type parameter that is not known yet.
options: Because {} means "an empty object", which has no null
Because {} is every value except null and undefined, so the intersection removes exactly those two

questions.q: A function has two overloads: (id: string): Booking and (ids: string[]): Booking[], in that order. What is its ReturnType?
questions.explain: When infer matches an overloaded function type, it uses the last signature. If you need the other result type, name it directly.

questions.q: What is Parameters<typeof quote> for function quote(zone: "lagos" | "abuja", weightKg: number, express = false)?
questions.explain: Parameters gives a labelled tuple. A parameter with a default value becomes an optional element, because callers may leave it out.
options: { zone: string; weightKg: number; express: boolean }

questions.q: Why is ReturnType<quoteDelivery> an error, when quoteDelivery is a function?
questions.explain: Utility types take types. typeof turns the function's name into its function type.
options: Because ReturnType only works on arrow functions
Because quoteDelivery is a value; the type argument must be a type, so write ReturnType<typeof quoteDelivery>
Because the function has no return annotation

questions.q: For class Room { constructor(name: string, priceKobo: number) {} }, what are ConstructorParameters<typeof Room> and InstanceType<typeof Room>?
questions.explain: Both take the constructor type, typeof Room: one extracts what new takes, the other what new gives, which is the instance type Room.
options: Both are errors, because Room is a class

questions.q: In type MyAwaited<T> = T extends PromiseLike<infer V> ? MyAwaited<V> : T, why does the true branch use MyAwaited<V> rather than V?
questions.explain: With just V, Promise<Promise<number>> would give Promise<number>. The recursion keeps unwrapping; Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>> is number.
options: To make the type slower to compute
So that nested promises are unwrapped repeatedly until no promise is left, like await
Because V alone is a syntax error

questions.q: What does ThisType<S & A> do when it appears in the type of an object literal's contextual type?
questions.explain: ThisType is an empty marker interface the compiler recognises (with noImplicitThis). It changes only the type of this; the runtime value of this still depends on how a method is called.
options: It binds the methods' this at runtime
It tells the compiler that this inside the literal's methods has type S & A
It adds the properties of S to the object at runtime

questions.q: For the public view of a user, why does the lesson prefer Pick<User, "id" | "name" | "role"> to Omit<User, "passwordHash">?
questions.explain: Deny-lists fail open: a new secret leaks until someone remembers to omit it. Allow-lists fail closed. Neither type changes the data; the view must still be built field by field.
options: Because with an allow-list, a field added to User later (say, a reset token) is not public until someone chooses to add it
Because Pick removes the fields from the object at runtime

questions.q: findUser is (id: string) => Promise<User | undefined>. What is NonNullable<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof findUser>>>?
questions.explain: Read from the inside out: ReturnType gives Promise<User | undefined>, Awaited removes the promise, and NonNullable removes undefined.

questions.q: Why is ReturnType's constraint T extends (...args: any) => any rather than (...args: unknown[]) => unknown?
questions.explain: Parameters are compared contravariantly: a function that needs a string cannot stand in for one that promises to accept anything. any in the parameter position switches that check off, so every function fits.
options: Because unknown did not exist when it was written
Because a function that takes specific parameters, such as (id: string) => User, is not assignable to one that must accept any unknown argument
Because any makes the result more precise
There is no reason; both work the same

questions.explain: A type annotation does not remove data. view is the same object as user, with all three properties; Pick only limits what the compiler lets you read.

questions.explain: ?? only replaces null and undefined, so a page size of 0 is kept. Required<ExportOptions> makes the compiler insist every option is filled in.

questions.explain: The wrapper logs first, then calls the original and returns its result. Parameters and ReturnType give fee the type (kobo: number, rate: number) => number.

questions.explain: build takes exactly the constructor's arguments and returns an instance, so coupon is a Coupon. Ten percent off ₦5,000 (500,000 kobo) is 450,000 kobo.

questions.explain: ThisType only types this; it does not bind it. A method taken off its object and called on its own has this set to undefined in a module, so reading balanceKobo throws. Called as wallet.balance(), it works.

questions.q: Finish withDefaults(options: Partial<ReportSettings>): Required<ReportSettings>. Defaults: currency "NGN", includeTax true, rounding 2. Keep falsy values that were given (such as 0 and false).
questions.explain: Partial for what callers pass, Required for what the rest of the code receives. ?? keeps false and 0; || would replace them.
questions.expected:
{ currency: 'NGN', includeTax: false, rounding: 0 }
{ currency: 'USD', includeTax: true, rounding: 2 }

questions.q: Write pickFields<T, K extends keyof T>(item: T, keys: readonly K[]): Pick<T, K> that builds a new object with only those keys, and use it for a room's public listing.
questions.explain: The starter returned the whole object, which the type allows, and leaked the cleaner's notes. The runtime copy makes the Pick type true. The one assertion is for the empty object that the loop fills.

questions.q: Write omitFields<T extends object, K extends keyof T>(item: T, keys: readonly K[]): Omit<T, K> that returns a copy without the given keys.
questions.explain: Copy, then delete from the copy, so the original is untouched. The K extends keyof T constraint makes a misspelt key a compile error, unlike the built-in Omit.

questions.q: Count orders per status into a Record<OrderStatus, number> that has an entry for every status, including those with no orders.
questions.explain: The starter's as claimed every status had a count when two were missing. Starting from a full Record makes the claim true, and the compiler checks that every status is initialized.

questions.q: Name the refund event with Extract, write the type guard isRefund, and print the total refunded kobo.
questions.explain: Extract picks the refund member by its discriminant, and the type predicate lets filter return RefundEvent[], so refund.amountKobo needs no check.

questions.q: Write counted<F extends (...args: any[]) => any>(fn: F): { call: (...args: Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F>; calls: () => number } that counts how often the wrapped function is called.
questions.explain: Parameters<F> and ReturnType<F> copy the wrapped function's signature, so vat.call is typed (kobo: number) => number. A closure keeps the count.

questions.q: Write buildAll<C extends new (...args: any[]) => any>(Class: C, rows: ConstructorParameters<C>[]): InstanceType<C>[] and use it to create products, then print their labels.
questions.explain: Each row must match the constructor's parameters, and the result is typed Product[], so product.label() is checked.

questions.q: Finish applyProfilePatch so it copies only name and city from the untrusted body, and only when they are strings. role in the body must be ignored.
questions.explain: The starter spread the whole body, so the customer became an admin and got a numeric name. The allow-list is the runtime half of Pick: fields outside it are never read.
